english: Then the question is whether there exists a definite family of closed curves (as circles for power series, ellipses, possibly lemniscates, for spherical functions) such that the curve of this family passing through the nearest singular point gives, i.e. encloses, the true region of convergence, so that the shape of the true convergence regions is essentially independent of the function being expanded.
topic: The page ends a note on a surface problem with a reference to Bianchi's theorem that fundamental quantities determine a surface, then asks whether a fixed family of closed curves bounds the true convergence region of expansions in a given series of analytic functions, and closes with questions inspired by Boy's surface: a 3-dimensional image of projective space in 4-space, and surfaces having a prescribed space curve as double curve.

triage.modern_statement: Take a fixed sequence of analytic functions (for example polynomials p_n) used to expand analytic functions f as f = Σ a_n p_n, where the coefficients depend on f. Is there a fixed family of nested closed curves, depending only on the expansion system and not on f, with the following property: for every f, the series converges exactly inside the curve of the family that passes through the singularity of f nearest the base set, and diverges outside it? Power series give circles. Legendre ('Kugelfunktion') series give confocal ellipses with foci ±1. In modern terms the question is whether 'maximal convergence' regions for a general system are bounded by the level curves of a fixed function. For polynomial systems attached to a compact set E, that function is the Green function of the complement of E, equivalently |Φ| for the exterior conformal map Φ (equipotential curves). Lemniscates are the level curves that occur when the reference set is a set of points or a lemniscatic domain.
triage.answered_by: For the natural classes of expansion systems this was answered affirmatively in the classical theory of maximal convergence. Faber (Faber polynomials, early 1900s), S. N. Bernstein and J. L. Walsh (the Bernstein–Walsh theory, developed by Walsh in the 1920s–30s and in his book 'Interpolation and Approximation by Rational Functions in the Complex Domain') showed that the right curves are the level curves (equipotentials) of the Green function or exterior conformal map of the reference set. Walsh's lemniscatic mapping theorem and Faber–Walsh polynomials extend this to multiply connected sets, where lemniscatic domains appear. For an arbitrary series of analytic functions there is no universal answer; the result depends on the system. I did not find a source that links this specific Hilbert note to these results. The names and dates of Faber, Bernstein and Walsh above come from general knowledge, not from the search results.

evidence.claim: Bernstein and Walsh developed a classical theory of maximal convergence for holomorphic functions in the complex plane, later extended to several variables.

Maximal convergence (Walsh): the rate of convergence improves with the analyticity of f. It is measured using the level curves Γ_R defined by |φ(z)| = R of the exterior conformal map, and has been studied for Faber series and Bergman orthogonal polynomial series.

Faber–Walsh polynomials depend only on the set E, not on f. The expansion Σ a_k b_k(z) converges in terms of level curves of the lemniscatic map, and when the exterior is a lemniscatic domain the basis polynomials reduce to lemniscate-type powers.
The convergence of Faber–Walsh expansions is governed by level curves of the lemniscatic map for multiply connected sets.

triage.why: Hilbert's question asks whether a fixed family of curves, depending only on the expansion system, governs convergence regions as circles do for power series and ellipses do for Legendre series. This is the founding idea of Faber/Bernstein–Walsh maximal convergence theory, where the answer is the equipotential (Green-function level) curves of the reference set; lemniscates appear in Walsh's multiply connected theory. Papers on Faber–Walsh polynomials and maximal convergence still appear recently, so the area is active. Confidence is medium for three reasons: Hilbert's question is broad (it says 'a given series of analytic functions'), no source ties this note to the later results, and some of the historical attributions come from general knowledge rather than the sources found.
